stem: Groundwork: find the clue that shows how the runners relate to thin air, then choose the phrase that names that relationship.
stimulus: Many of the runners in the study had never trained at high altitude before. Being ______ thin mountain air, they tired quickly during the first week, and their coaches shortened every workout until the runners' bodies had time to adjust.
explanation: The clue is "had never trained at high altitude before," and "until the runners' bodies had time to adjust" confirms it. The text describes a lack of experience. It says nothing about feelings. "Unaccustomed to" means exactly that: not used to something. This is the first step in every Words in Context question where each choice ends in a preposition. Before you look at the choices, decide what kind of relationship the text describes (feeling, skill, or experience) and whether it is positive or negative.

A.why: You picked a strong emotion that suits a story about struggling athletes. The text never says the runners were angry, only that they were not used to the air. This is the trap of matching the mood of the topic instead of the logic.

C.why: You got the direction backwards. Runners who had never trained at altitude and tired quickly are the opposite of skilled in thin air.

D.why: You added a feeling the text never mentions, and a positive one too. Nothing in the passage says the runners liked the mountain air. It says they were not used to it.

stem: Groundwork: find the clue that shows how early mapmakers treated secondhand reports, then choose the phrase that names that relationship.
stimulus: Early mapmakers were often ______ secondhand reports. Rather than leaving unknown coastlines blank, they drew in whatever shapes sailors described to them, even when the descriptions were vague. This willingness to accept hearsay filled many maps with bays and islands that did not exist.
explanation: The sentence after the blank tells you what the blank means. The mapmakers drew whatever sailors described, and the text calls this a "willingness to accept hearsay." That is openness, and "receptive to" means open to accepting something. On real questions the definition of the blank often comes in the next sentence, so read past the blank before you choose.

A.why: You reversed the relationship. Mapmakers who drew in even vague descriptions were accepting those reports, not doubting them.

B.why: You were drawn to a vivid, strong reaction. The text describes mapmakers who readily accepted reports, not mapmakers who were angry about them. This is the trap of choosing the most dramatic phrase.

D.why: You chose a phrase about skill, but the text describes openness: a willingness to accept. Having experience with reports is a different relationship from being willing to believe them.

stem: Groundwork: find the clue that shows how cleaner wrasses relate to removing parasites, then choose the phrase that names that relationship.
stimulus: Cleaner wrasses are ______ removing parasites from larger fish. A single wrasse can pick hundreds of tiny parasites from visiting fish in one day, working quickly around the gills and mouth without harming its much bigger clients.
explanation: The second sentence gives the evidence: hundreds of parasites removed in a day, quick work, and no harm done. That is a description of ability, and "skilled at" names ability. Many real questions of this type turn on one question: does the text describe a feeling or a skill? Here the evidence is all performance and no emotion.

A.why: You chose an excited, vivid phrase that sounds lively. The text shows what the wrasse can do, not how it feels. Nothing supports the idea that it is thrilled. This is the trap of picking a strong emotion when the logic calls for ability.

B.why: You reversed the evidence. A fish that removes hundreds of parasites quickly and safely is clearly familiar with the job.

D.why: You latched onto "larger fish" and assumed fear. The text says the wrasse works right around the gills and mouth of its bigger clients, which is the opposite of fear.

stem: Groundwork: find the clue that shows what planners once expected from residents, then choose the phrase that names that relationship.
stimulus: City planners once assumed that residents would be ______ new bike lanes on their streets, and they expected a wave of complaints about lost parking spaces. But surveys in several cities found the opposite: most residents welcomed the lanes and asked for more of them.
explanation: The blank sits inside the old assumption, the view that the surveys later overturn. The planners "expected a wave of complaints," so they assumed residents would push back. "Resistant to" names that mild opposition. On real questions, check which side of a "but" reversal the blank is on. Here it is on the planners' mistaken side, so it means the opposite of what the surveys found.

A.why: You took the answer from the wrong side of the reversal. Residents being eager is what the surveys found. The blank describes what planners wrongly expected before the surveys.

C.why: You chose a phrase far stronger than the evidence allows. Complaints about parking show opposition, not fear. This is the trap of picking the most dramatic reaction when the text supports a milder one.

D.why: You chose a phrase about ability, but the sentence is about residents' attitude toward the lanes. Whether someone is skilled at something has nothing to do with whether they would complain about it.
